sb_prompt: WHAT ADVICE OR EXPERIENCE CAN YOU OFFER TO A PARENT ON HOW TO HELP A SON OR DAUGHTER CHOOSE A COLLEGE TO ATTEND?
turns: Yeah, I'm actually in a pretty tough spot right now, my cousin's kid is getting out of high school this year and we're trying to figure out where to send him.
Yeah, that sounds stressful. I mean, my own kid's already at a community college and I'm not sure he's ever going to finish, so I get why you're worried about picking the right place.

Yeah, well, it's not just me he's for, it's my cousin who actually went through the whole mess of applying to places like Harvard and got rejected, so I'm kind of stuck between wanting him to have the "top" school and knowing that might just be a waste of money.
Yeah, honestly? I kind of feel that way about my son. I mean, the tuition for that private school he's looking at... it's just so much he'll never earn. I guess I just don't see why he needs it.

Yeah, that's exactly what my cousin's parents keep saying, though they still feel bad about the rejection because he really wanted to go there. But honestly, my cousin did get a full ride at a state school and he's already hired at a local grocery chain, so maybe that's a better path?

Yeah, but I guess I just worry he's gonna be stuck working minimum wage forever, you know? Like, I hate to say it, but my son is already doing the same thing at the store—just stocking shelves instead of managing them. It feels like a dead end to me, honestly. I mean, we put so much time and money into his education just to have him back here doing the same jobs?

Wait, hold on, I get that, but my cousin's working his way through school right now because the full ride covered tuition and books, and honestly, he's already got a manager position lined up at the chain.

Wait, hold on a sec. If he's the manager, isn't that a big step up? I mean, I'm just the receptionist here, so I don't have to manage people, I just answer phones. But honestly, seeing my kid stuck in the same spot as the stock boys... it makes me want to give up on him too. Like, why bother with the degree if he's just gonna be buying milk?
Yeah, it's not just buying milk, it's managing the whole floor, scheduling the guys, dealing with the inventory issues, and honestly, the stress of it all is real.

It sounds like a real upgrade from just restocking, I'll admit. But still, I've got this feeling that unless he's got some real drive to keep climbing, he might just end up doing the same thing his dad does, just with a fancier title.

Yeah, it's a lot of responsibility, but look, I've seen it happen. My cousin's actual boss there is a guy who made the same mistake—went to some fancy school, came back, couldn't keep up, and ended up working the overnight shift at the same store we're both in. He's just stocking shelves now. So, you know, the degree doesn't guarantee you won't end up doing what your dad does, but it sure makes the jump from the floor to the back office much easier if you have that experience under your belt.

Yeah, but I'm still scared he's gonna be just like that guy, you know? All the stress and the hours... and honestly, it feels like we're just paying for him to learn how to run a register faster than I do.

I get that fear, but honestly, the guy who ended up stocking shelves? He has no idea how to talk to anyone, let alone a customer, and that's the first thing I had to teach him before he could even open the register.
Yeah, but I still think teaching him to talk to people is a waste if he's not gonna learn something about a different field, like maybe accounting or something where he actually moves up the ladder.

Look, you're thinking too much about the title and not enough about the actual work. I'm down there on the floor with these guys every single day, and honestly, if you don't know how to talk to a customer or handle a refund, you're not gonna last a year in this job no matter what your degree says. That guy you're scared of? He quit after three months because he couldn't deal with a kid who dropped his milk, and the manager couldn't even fire him because he had to wait for corporate approval. So yeah, maybe the degree won't make him rich, but it sure won't make him stuck in the same spot as his dad, because he'll actually know how to get through the day without crying every time someone asks for a different kind of yogurt.

Yeah, but what if he hates dealing with people anyway? I mean, I spend my whole day on the phone just trying to keep customers happy, and honestly, sometimes it feels like talking to a wall, so if he's gonna be out there shouting at kids who drop milk, I don't know if he's gonna make it. Plus, if he does end up in accounting, at least then he's working with numbers, right? And I hear his dad say, "You just need to learn to count," so maybe he could be the guy who actually does the math behind the scenes instead of the yelling on the floor?

That's a fair point about the personality fit, but let me tell you, that specific guy who quit? He didn't even know how to open the register, and the manager had to step in and show him the whole process because the kid literally didn't know how to take the card terminal apart if it was giving an error.

Yeah, but that sounds like way too much pressure for a kid who's just starting out, doesn't it? And honestly, if he's gonna be stressed out opening registers all day, maybe he should just stick with the math stuff I'm good at, or at least look into something that doesn't involve people yelling at him.
Yeah, but if he's scared of people he can't take the shift, then the degree is useless because he's gonna quit and end up back where we started anyway.
Yeah, but if he hates the people part, then he's just gonna quit again and end up doing exactly what his dad does, which is the whole point I'm trying to avoid.

I get where you're coming from, but honestly, the point of the degree is giving him the chance to walk into an interview and not get laughed out of the room, whereas that guy you're talking about? He didn't even have the basic know-how to show up on time, and that's what really kills it for us.

That's a lot to expect from a kid just starting out, honestly. I mean, what if he's good with numbers but terrible with talking? Then he's stuck in accounting doing the same math his dad does, just behind a desk.
Look, you're missing the point—it's not about the subject, it's about the interview itself, because without that degree, he's just another guy in the back wearing that uniform nobody notices.
Yeah, but if he's stuck in accounting doing the same math his dad does, just behind a desk, then what's the point of the degree anyway?

I get it, you're worried about the dead end, but look, if he doesn't have that degree, he's not even applying for the accounting jobs where he'd actually be working with numbers, he's just the one doing the counting on the register because nobody else wants to do the work.
Yeah, but if he's stuck in accounting doing the same math his dad does, just behind a desk, then what's the point of the degree anyway?

You keep saying the same thing, which tells me you really don't get it—the point isn't that he's doing math, it's that with the degree, he gets hired for the job where the math matters, not the job where the math is just something you do to keep your own desk from getting messy.

Yeah, but I still think that's just you selling it to yourself, because if he ends up hating the people part, the degree won't save him from being miserable, and honestly, sitting at a desk doing math while your dad's name is on the door above you doesn't really fix the problem either.

I get that, but listen, you're stuck on the "hate people" part, and that's exactly where the degree saves him—he's not going to yell at kids, he's going to talk to them like an adult because he's educated, whereas that guy who quit? He was yelling because he didn't know how to handle the situation, and the degree teaches you how to de-escalate, which is the only way you survive in this job without crying.

Yeah, but if he's gonna be dealing with people all day, isn't he just gonna learn to yell instead of think? And honestly, if he ends up hating it and quits, he's just gonna end up stocking shelves like his dad anyway, so why not just stick with the numbers where he won't have to talk to anyone?
Look, if he hates people, he quits, and that's exactly what I'm trying to stop.
Yeah, but if he quits again, we're just back at square one, aren't we?

I mean, if he quits, the degree doesn't matter because nobody hires people who can't take a hard shift, so the only way he stays employed at all is if he learns the soft skills to keep his job, otherwise he's stocking shelves tomorrow and we're back to square one.

I guess I just don't see how talking to people is gonna save him if he hates them that much, because honestly, once he quits, the degree gets thrown out the window and we're just paying for four years of nothing while he sits at a desk doing my dad's math.

Look, you keep looking at this as an "either/or" situation, but it's not just about the subject or the people; it's that the degree is what keeps him employed long enough to actually learn the skills you think he needs, because if he quits after three months like that guy did, you're right, it's all for nothing, but if he stays, the degree is what gets him promoted before your dad gets promoted, which is the whole point of doing it in the first place.

I mean, if he quits after three months, you're right, it's all for nothing, but if he stays, the degree is what gets him promoted before your dad gets promoted, which is the whole point of doing it in the first place.

I get you're worried about the investment, but look, if he's got the degree, he doesn't have to worry about *your* name on the door above him, he walks in as an equal or better than you, and that changes the whole dynamic of the conversation.
If he gets promoted before your dad, does that mean he'll actually have a real job, or is it just the same work with a nicer badge?

Look, if he's got the degree, he walks in as an equal or better than you, and that changes the whole dynamic of the conversation.
If he gets promoted before your dad, does that mean he'll actually have a real job, or is it just the same work with a nicer badge?
I mean, if it's just a nicer badge, what's the point of spending our savings on it?
